up.e: From Middle English up, op, oup, from Old English upp, up, ūp (“up”), from Proto-West Germanic *upp, *ūp, from Proto-Germanic *upp, *eup (“up”).
up.g: Indicating movement towards or location at a higher place or position.

upbraid.e: From Middle English upbreiden, from Old English upbreġdan, equivalent to up- + braid.

uphold.e: From Middle English upholden, equivalent to up- + hold.
uphold.g: To hold up; to lift on high; to elevate.

uplift.g: To raise something or someone to a higher physical, social, moral, intellectual, spiritual, or emotional level.

upper.e: From Middle English upper. By surface analysis, up + -er.
upper.g: At a higher physical position, level, rank or order.

uppermost.e: From Middle English upper-moste; equivalent to upper + -most.
uppermost.g: superlative form of upper: most upper.

upraise.g: To raise something up; to elevate.

upright.e: From Middle English upright, uppryght, upriht, from Old English upriht (“upright; erect”), from Proto-Germanic *upprehtaz, equivalent to up- + right.

uprising.g: A popular revolt that attempts to overthrow a government or its policies; an insurgency or insurrection.

uproar.e: Calque of Dutch oproer or German Aufruhr, as up + roar.

uproot.e: From up- (prefix indicating a higher direction or position) + root (“to tear up by the roots; (figuratively) to remove forcibly from a place; to eradicate, exterminate”, verb). Root is derived from root (“underground part of a plant”, noun), from Middle English rote, from Old English rōt, rōte, from Old Norse rót.
uproot.g: To tear up (a plant, etc.) by the roots, or as if by the roots; to extirpate, to root up.

uproot.e: From up- (prefix indicating a higher direction or position) + root (“of a pig or other animal: to dig or turn up with the snout; to search as if by digging in soil, rummage”, verb). Root is derived from Middle English wroten (“to dig or turn up with the snout; to remove soil, dig up”), from Old English wrōtan (“to dig or turn up with the snout”).
uproot.g: Of a pig or other animal: to dig up (something in the ground) using the snout; to rummage for (something) in the ground; to grub up, to root

upset.e: From Middle English upset (“the act of setting up; establishment”), from Middle English upsetten, corresponding to up- + set.

upside.g: The highest or uppermost side or portion of something.

upward.e: From Old English upweardes, equivalent to up + -ward.
upward.g: In a direction from lower to higher; toward a higher place; in a course toward the source or origin.
